opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing to recognize is that academia isn't going to win by competing head-on with industry on scale. We don't have the compute, the data, or the engineering teams to train frontier models, and trying to play that game is mostly a losing proposition. But that's not where academia's comparative advantage lies anyway.

Where I think we can contribute most is in the areas industry has weak incentives to do well. Evaluation is a big one. Companies have every reason to report benchmark numbers that make their models look good. Someone independent has to ask whether those benchmarks measure anything meaningful, whether there's contamination, and whether performance in a controlled setting translates to real-world usefulness. A lot of the hype cycle comes from that gap between benchmark results and real deployment, and academics are well placed to study it rigorously.

A second area is understanding AI's impacts on people and institutions: what happens when these systems are deployed in hiring, healthcare, education, criminal justice. That's inherently interdisciplinary. It needs computer scientists working with social scientists, legal scholars, and domain experts, and universities are one of the few places where that collaboration happens naturally.

Third, academics can play a critical role in separating what works from what doesn't. There's a lot of AI being sold that simply doesn't do what it claims, especially predictive tools that promise to forecast things like job performance or criminal risk. Being able to say clearly, with evidence, "this works, this doesn't, and here's why" is enormously valuable to policymakers and the public.

And finally, I'd say there's value in the slower, more foundational work: building conceptual frameworks, asking questions that won't pay off in a product cycle, and training the next generation of researchers to think critically rather than just chase leaderboards. So academia's role isn't diminished in this era. It's just different, and arguably more important than ever.

r001.rationale: The response recommends focusing on areas where industry has weak incentives, implying companies may be able to do the work but are unlikely to prioritize it.

r002.rationale: It identifies independent evaluation of benchmarks as a major area where academics can contribute.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that academics are not going to win at building the biggest models, and we should stop pretending that's the game we're in. The compute and data advantages of industry labs are enormous, and chasing them is a losing proposition.

Where academics have a real comparative advantage is in asking the questions that companies have no incentive to ask. One is evaluation and scrutiny. Who is checking whether these systems actually work in the settings they're deployed in? When we looked at things like predictive models in criminal justice, or hiring, or medicine, the gap between the benchmark claims and real-world performance was often dramatic. Industry has every reason to overstate; academia can be the adversarial check.

A second is studying AI as it meets society. What happens when a chatbot is used by millions of people for medical questions, or when generative models flood the information ecosystem? These are empirical questions that require independence from the vendors, and often require methods from the social sciences, not just computer science.

Third, I'd point to the long-term, unglamorous stuff: reproducibility, documentation, teaching the next generation of researchers to be skeptical. A lot of the hype cycle in machine learning comes from a leakage of poor scientific practice, and universities are the place to fix that.

And finally, I'd say academics should feel free to be slow and contrarian. Industry has to ship. We don't. That freedom to say "wait, is this actually true?" is the most valuable thing we have, and we should use it more.

r001.rationale: The response says academics should ask questions companies have no incentive to ask, framing this as a comparative advantage despite companies’ ability to build the systems.

r002.rationale: It identifies evaluation as an academic contribution and discusses checking systems against benchmark claims and real-world performance.

astra-6.text:
I think academia has the most to contribute by asking questions that industry doesn’t have strong incentives to ask. It’s difficult for most academic labs to compete with industry on training the largest models. But that doesn’t mean we should treat everything else as secondary.

One important role is independent evaluation. What can these systems actually do? Where do they fail? And do the benchmarks we use tell us anything meaningful about how they’ll perform in the real world? Those questions require careful research, and the answers may not align with the interests of the companies building the systems.

There’s also a much broader set of questions about how AI interacts with people and institutions. If you introduce an AI system into education or health care, the model’s accuracy alone doesn’t tell you whether it’s useful. You have to understand how people use it, how it changes their decisions, and who benefits or bears the costs. That’s an area where interdisciplinary academic research can contribute a lot.

So I’d like to see academic researchers feel more comfortable setting their own agenda, including questioning the assumptions behind the problems industry has chosen to pursue.

r001.rationale: The response says academia should ask questions that industry lacks strong incentives to ask and encourages researchers to set their own agenda, clearly recommending work companies may be capable of doing but unlikely to prioritize.

r002.rationale: It explicitly questions whether benchmarks meaningfully predict real-world performance as part of independent evaluation, identifying benchmarking as a significant research contribution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think academic researchers can contribute most by asking questions that industry has less incentive to ask. If you’re at a company, your research agenda is naturally shaped by the products you’re building. In academia, we have the freedom to step back and ask: Are we measuring the right things? Where do these systems fail? And what happens when people actually use them?

That doesn’t necessarily require training a bigger model. It might require a carefully designed experiment, a better evaluation, or studying a particular deployment in depth. There’s a lot of room to contribute by making our understanding of AI more rigorous—especially by testing claims that have become widely accepted without much evidence.

r001.rationale: The response says academia can pursue questions industry has less incentive to ask because company research is shaped by products, indicating work companies could do but are unlikely to prioritize.

r002.rationale: It mentions measurement and better evaluation, but does not clearly identify benchmarking as a contribution area.
